Compiling WebAssembly Concolic Execution with Staging, Continuations, and Snapshots (Extended Version)Note:  This paper is an extended version of the paper of the same title published at OOPSLA 2026. Its appendix includes complete definitions of the formal semantics and algorithms.

Abstract.

Concolic execution is a variant of symbolic execution that runs a program simultaneously with concrete and symbolic inputs. It records the symbolic constraints encountered along a concrete execution path, then solves those constraints to generate inputs that explore new paths. Existing concolic engines generally follow one of two implementation strategies: Interpreter-based systems are comparatively simple to build but incur substantial interpretation overhead, while instrumentation-based systems avoid this overhead but typically re-execute the program from the beginning for each new input.

In this paper, we develop a new approach that achieves the best of both worlds. Starting from the concrete semantics of the target language, we first develop a definitional concolic interpreter and stage it to compile away interpretation overhead while retaining the simplicity of an interpretation-based implementation. By expressing the staged interpreter in continuation-passing style, we can capture execution snapshots at branch points and resume from them when exploring alternative paths, avoiding repeated execution from the program entry. Because snapshot-reuse can itself incur overhead, we further develop a heuristic that favors snapshot-reuse only when it is expected to be beneficial. We instantiate this approach for WebAssembly and implement it in a new concolic-execution compiler GenWasym. Across 184 benchmarks, GenWasym with staging alone achieves a 29.4×29.4\times average speedup over the interpreter-based WASP; heuristic snapshot-reuse further increases the speedup to 44.9×44.9\times.

Keywords: 
Concolic execution, Continuation, WebAssembly, Semantics, Staging, Performance

1. Introduction

As a white-box testing technique, modern symbolic execution (SE) (Cadar and Sen, 2013) automates test generation and bug finding by partitioning the input space of programs and utilizing the power of SMT solvers (Barrett et al., 2021). By treating some inputs as symbolic values (Boyer et al., 1975; King, 1976; Howden, 1977; Clarke, 1976), symbolic execution calculates the conditions of program paths symbolically. These conditions represent equivalence classes of inputs that can trigger the execution of specific paths. General nondeterministic symbolic execution (e.g., KLEE (Cadar et al., 2008), GenSym (Wei et al., 2023)) forks the execution and explores multiple paths simultaneously. However, this approach requires frequent path feasibility checks and quickly leads to path explosion.

Concolic execution (Godefroid et al., 2005; Sen et al., 2005; Godefroid et al., 2008) alleviates solver overhead and path explosion by constraining itself to run only one path at a time, guided by a concrete input. Since path feasibility is evidenced by that concrete input, it suffices to collect the corresponding path condition without querying solvers when running the program. In this way, concolic execution mixes concrete and symbolic execution. After executing one path, new inputs are generated by negating parts of the collected path condition and solving satisfiability for the new concrete inputs. These new inputs lead the engine to explore new paths in the program. A driver orchestrates this process iteratively to systematically explore the program space. In practice, concolic execution is often more effective for bug finding and is the building block of widely adopted hybrid fuzzing techniques (Majumdar and Sen, 2007; Yun et al., 2018; Stephens et al., 2016), as concrete inputs can drive execution deep into the program.

Interpretation or Instrumentation?

Concolic execution can be viewed as a specific “path scheduling strategy”, where the path to be explored is biased by the concrete inputs provided in each iteration. However, in each iteration with a new input, concolic execution needs to rerun the program from the beginning (i.e., the root of the symbolic execution tree), both concretely and symbolically. Although a prefix of the execution is shared between the paths explored by the new and old inputs, the corresponding path conditions for the new path must still be re-collected through unnecessary re-execution. This redundant re-execution hurts performance and throughput of concolic execution, especially when the negation point lies deep in the execution tree.

Indeed, re-execution can be avoided by reusing the existing symbolic state from the negation point, an optimization known as snapshot reuse (e.g., Driller (Stephens et al., 2016)). It has been observed that Driller with snapshot reuse achieves more coverage in 76 out of 126 benchmarks from DARPA’s Cyber Grand Challenge (Yun et al., 2018). Realizing snapshot reuse requires copying the program state and saving it at the corresponding branching point, so that in the next iteration, execution can directly jump back to that point and continue the alternative branch. Due to these requirements, implementing snapshot reuse is most straightforward within interpretation-based concolic execution, where the engine has full control over the execution state and control flow at the meta level. However, copying the whole program state can be expensive (Yun et al., 2018), and interpretation imposes significant overhead (Jones et al., 1993), such as traversing and dispatching over the program’s static AST/IR. These overheads make interpretation a less ideal choice for performance-critical concolic execution, even with snapshot reuse.

To achieve high performance, state-of-the-art concolic execution engines (e.g., QSYM (Yun et al., 2018) for binaries, SymCC (Poeplau and Francillon, 2020) for LLVM IR, and SymQEMU (Poeplau and Francillon, 2021) for VEX IR) rely on source-to-source instrumentation to completely avoid interpretation overhead. Since concolic execution explores only one path at a time, instrumentation needs only to insert symbolic instructions that collect path conditions alongside the control flow of the original concrete execution. However, these instrumentation-based engines abandon snapshot reuse at all. It is no coincidence: with instrumentation that shallowly inserts additional instructions, the program itself cannot save its current control at a branching point 11 1 To be precise, it would require the language to have mechanisms such as call/cc to capture the current continuation, which is not the case here for typical targets of concolic execution. and later resume it in the next iteration. Therefore, it is challenging to implement snapshot reuse entirely within instrumentation-based concolic execution.

Best of Two Worlds

Although instrumentation enables fast execution, snapshot reuse remains a valuable optimization, especially when branch points occur deep in the execution. To maximize throughput, these two techniques should be combined. Existing implementation strategies, however, force concolic-execution engine designers to choose between them: snapshot reuse is relatively straightforward to implement in an interpreter, but incurs substantial interpretation overhead; instrumentation eliminates that overhead, but makes snapshot reuse difficult to realize.

In this paper, we resolve this tension by showing how to obtain instrumentation-like performance while still supporting effective snapshot reuse. Our key idea is to partially evaluate (Jones et al., 1993) a concolic interpreter written in continuation-passing style (CPS) (Reynolds, 1993; Appel, 1992) using staging (Taha and Sheard, 1997; Taha, 1999; Rompf and Odersky, 2010).

  • •

    By staging a concolic interpreter, we specialize it with respect to the input program and thereby generate efficient concolic-execution code that no longer suffers from interpretation overhead, achieving instrumentation-like performance. In effect, our approach realizes compilation via the first Futamura projection (Futamura, 1971; Futamura, 1999) for a concolic interpreter. At the same time, constructing a concolic interpreter is arguably simpler than building a compiler, so our approach reduces the implementation effort required for high-performance engines.

  • •

    By writing the staged concolic interpreter in CPS, we make control flow explicit and manipulable as first-class functions in the generated code, which enables snapshot reuse. At each branch in the source program, we generate code that stores the current state and continuation as a snapshot. When execution later resumes from that branch point, the engine invokes the saved continuation for the alternative branch, completely avoiding re-execution from the program entry to that point.

Applying staging or partial evaluation to program analysis is not new (Damian, 1999; Amtoft, 1999; Wei et al., 2019; Boucher and Feeley, 1996; Wei et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2023), nor is the use of continuations in symbolic execution engines (Wei et al., 2023). Our work is inspired in part by GenSym’s metaprogramming approach (Wei et al., 2023), which shows that, for nondeterministic symbolic execution of LLVM IR, continuations can be used to implement search heuristics. We adopt the idea of using continuations to manipulate control flow at the meta level. To the best of our knowledge, however, this is the first work to combine staging and continuations in a concolic execution engine to achieve both high execution performance and snapshot reuse, unifying two optimizations that have previously been deployed only separately in practice.

That said, the effectiveness of snapshot reuse still depends on the target program. When symbolic states are large and execution paths are shallow, saving and restoring snapshots can cost more than simply re-executing from the beginning, since the avoided re-execution may be minimal. To address this trade-off, we propose a heuristic that decides when to use snapshots based on execution depth and symbolic-state complexity (Section 6). Our heuristic also avoids using snapshots for external functions, which may have side effects depending on the concrete inputs. With this heuristic, our approach smoothly combines the best of both worlds: efficient execution through compilation and adaptive snapshot reuse via continuations when it is likely to pay off.

Compiled Concolic Execution with Snapshots for WebAssembly

To demonstrate and validate our approach, we use WebAssembly (Wasm) (Haas et al., 2017) as the target language. As a general-purpose, low-level bytecode language, WebAssembly has emerged as an important target for both compilation and program analysis. WebAssembly is now supported by all major browsers and has also been adopted beyond the browser setting.

Despite WebAssembly’s growing importance, existing concolic or symbolic execution tools for Wasm remain interpreter-based, limiting their performance and scalability. To the best of our knowledge, there is no instrumentation- or compilation-based concolic execution engine for Wasm. Therefore, our focus on Wasm is motivated both by its growing importance as a deployment and analysis target and by the current lack of high-performance concolic execution tools for it.

We present our development through a sequence of mechanical derivation steps, each obtained from the previous one. We begin with a concrete continuation-passing semantics for WebAssembly (Section 2), formulated as a definitional interpreter (Reynolds, 1972) adapted from (Wei et al., 2025). On top of this foundation, we derive a concolic evaluator in CPS (Section 3), refactor it into a staged concolic interpreter in CPS (Section 4), and finally show how snapshots can be reused in the generated code (Section 5).

Although this paper focuses on WebAssembly as the target language, our approach is not specific to WebAssembly and readily extends to other languages or intermediate representations (Section 9). Our mechanical, derivational methodology helps ensure that each step is correct by construction and makes the overall approach easier to transfer to other languages.

Implementation and Evaluation

We implement our architecture in GenWasym, a concolic-execution compiler for Wasm written in Scala using LMS (Rompf and Odersky, 2010). Given a Wasm program, GenWasym generates a C++ implementation following our snapshot-reusing concolic semantics. The generated program links against a scheduler that invokes the SMT solver to generate new inputs and applies our heuristic (Section 6), which chooses between re-execution and applying snapshots. To the best of our knowledge, GenWasym is the first concolic-execution compiler for Wasm and the first Wasm concolic engine to support snapshot reuse.

We evaluate GenWasym against WASP (Marques et al., 2022), the prior state-of-the-art concolic execution engine for WebAssembly. WASP suffers from two performance limitations due to its design as an interpreter-based engine. First, it is built on the reference small-step reduction semantics (Haas et al., 2017), which incurs substantial interpretation cost when resolving control flow, such as jumps, through administrative instructions (Watt et al., 2023). Second, it does not support snapshot reuse, leading to redundant re-execution. Our work addresses both limitations.

We evaluate GenWasym on the B-Tree benchmark suite and the Collections-C benchmark suite (srdja, n.d.) used by WASP (Marques et al., 2022). Across 184 benchmarks, GenWasym with staging alone achieves an average (geomean) speedup of 29.4×29.4\times. Further enabling heuristic snapshot reuse yields an average speedup of 44.9×44.9\times. The results show that staging uniformly eliminates the majority overhead from interpretation, yielding orders-of-magnitude speedups, while on top of that snapshot reuse provides significant additional improvement for programs with deep execution paths.

Contributions and Organization

In this paper, we develop the first concolic-execution architecture to combine high-performance execution with snapshot reuse, enabled by the key insight of using staging with continuations in the concolic-execution engine. We demonstrate our approach with Wasm, implement the snapshot-reusing concolic-execution compiler GenWasym, and evaluate its performance through extensive experiments. The paper is organized as follows:

  • •

    Section 2 briefly reviews concolic execution, Wasm, and Wasm’s concrete CPS semantics.

  • •

    Section 3 develops a definitional concolic interpreter based on the concrete CPS semantics. Section 4 derives the staged concolic interpreter by refactoring the single-stage concolic interpreter.

  • •

    Section 5 explains how to implement snapshot reuse (i.e., avoiding re-execution) in the generated concolic execution code by manipulating continuations. Section 6 proposes a heuristic to decide when to reuse snapshots to balance the benefit and cost of snapshot resumption.

  • •

    Section 7 describes our implementation of GenWasym, which is implemented in Scala and generates C++ code for concolic execution of WebAssembly programs.

  • •

    Section 8 presents the performance evaluation of GenWasym against WASP (Marques et al., 2022), showing an average 29.4×29.4\times speedup. We also evaluate the effectiveness of our snapshot heuristic.

  • •

    Section 9 compares our approach with instrumentation and discusses its applicability to other languages; Section 10 reviews related work; and Section 11 concludes the paper.

2. Background

In this section, we provide background on concolic execution, WebAssembly, and its CPS semantics (Wei et al., 2025) that we build upon.

2.1. Concolic Execution

Concolic execution (Ball and Daniel, 2015; Godefroid et al., 2005; Sen et al., 2005; Godefroid et al., 2008) runs program pp with concrete input ii, traces an execution path π\pi, and collects its path condition cond. Solving negated path condition ¬cond\neg\textit{cond} with an SMT solver generates a new input i′i^{\prime} that explores a another path. This process repeats until all paths are explored or a limit (e.g., time or coverage) is reached.

Consider the example program and its execution tree shown in Figure 1. Suppose we start concolic execution with initial inputs x=3x=3 and y=5y=5. The execution path in orange collects the path condition x>0∧y>0∧x2+y2≠25x>0\land y>0\land x^{2}+y^{2}\neq 25 along the way. To explore a new path, concolic execution negates the condition, e.g., x>0∧y>0∧x2+y2=25x>0\land y>0\land x^{2}+y^{2}=25 where the last condition is negated, and queries the SMT solver for a new input satisfying the negated condition. The solver returns a new input x=4x=4 and y=3y=3, which explores a new path shown in blue in Figure 1. However, to reach the error node in the blue path, the concolic execution engine needs to re-execute part of the program, which was already executed in the last iteration. If the underlying concolic execution engine can save the snapshot at branch points, it can reuse those symbolic states to avoid re-execution.

The topic of this paper is to develop an approach to concolic execution that is easy to implement, efficient to execute, and able to reuse symbolic states to avoid re-execution.

2.2. WebAssembly

We demonstrate our approach on WebAssembly, an emerging portable stack-based virtual instruction set for safe and efficient execution on the web and beyond. In the formalization, we limit our discussion to μ\muWasm, a subset of WebAssembly that captures the core features relevant to concolic execution. Readers may refer to the official specification (Rossberg, 2022) for more details about WebAssembly. Figure 2 shows the syntax of μ\muWasm, and Figure 3 shows its concrete semantics. μ\muWasm models the following instructions covering the essential part of local variables, control flow, and function calls in WebAssembly:

  • •

    We model a range of arithmetic instructions. For example, t.𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍​ct.\mathsf{const}~c pushes a constant value cc of type tt onto the stack, and t.𝖺𝖽𝖽t.\mathsf{add} pops two operands of type tt from the stack, then pushes the addition result back to the stack. Instruction 𝗅𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅.𝗀𝖾𝗍​x\mathsf{local.get}~x pushes the value of variable xx onto the stack, and 𝗅𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅.𝗌𝖾𝗍​x\mathsf{local.set}~x sets the value of variable xx using the top value on the stack.

  • •

    Unlike most other low-level IRs, WebAssembly supports structured control flow with 𝖻𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄\mathsf{block}, 𝗅𝗈𝗈𝗉\mathsf{loop}, and 𝗂𝖿\mathsf{if} instructions, containing sequences of instructions as their bodies. Since block-like instructions can be nested, WebAssembly uses the 𝖻𝗋​l\mathsf{br}~l instruction to transfer control-flow to the target block, where label ll is the de Bruijn index identifying the target block. Block-like instructions are annotated with a function type tm→tnt^{m}\to t^{n}, indicating the shape of the stack before and after the execution of the block.

  • •

    A top-level program consists of a module of functions. Each function has an identifier, a type, a list of local variables, and a sequence of instructions as its body. The instruction 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅​x\mathsf{call}~x transfers the control-flow to the callee, and 𝗋𝖾𝗍𝗎𝗋𝗇\mathsf{return} transfers the control-flow back to the caller.

We omit typing of the language, which is standard and can be found in the official WebAssembly specification (Rossberg, 2022). We also omit Wasm features such as tables, global variables, and memory, which are not essential to explain our approach. However, our implementation in Section 7 supports a larger subset of WebAssembly and can handle more realistic programs.

2.3. Continuation-Passing Semantics of μ\muWasm

Why Continuations?

The official WebAssembly specification (Rossberg, 2022) defines a small-step reduction semantics. However, the semantics has to introduce administrative instructions to manage control flow; these instructions represent evaluation contexts and are materialized only at runtime. This obscures the binding-time distinction between parts of the program that are known at compile time and others at runtime, rendering it difficult to construct a staged interpreter on top of it.

In this paper, we adopt a continuation-passing semantics (Wei et al., 2025) for WebAssembly that is defined in a compositional way using continuation functions to represent control flow. It is well-known that continuations improve binding-time separation, allowing more computation to be evaluated at compile time (Lawall and Danvy, 1994; Holst and Gomard, 1991; Consel and Danvy, 1991). We later exploit this insight and build the staged concolic interpreter on top of the CPS semantics (Wei et al., 2025). Moreover, continuations naturally model the snapshots of symbolic states needed for concolic execution, as we will discuss in Section 5.

The correctness of the CPS semantics could be established by relating it to the small-step semantics via defunctionalization (Danvy and Millikin, 2009) and refunctionalization (Danvy and Nielsen, 2001; Gibbons, 2022). A detailed investigation of this connection is out of the scope of this work.

CPS Semantics of μ\muWasm

Figure 3 shows μ\muWasm’s concrete CPS semantics (Wei et al., 2025). Values are represented as integers, and stack and environment are both lists of values. We call the current stack and environment the program state. Continuations κ\kappa are represented as functions from states to the final result 𝖠𝗇𝗌\mathsf{Ans}. The 𝖠𝗇𝗌\mathsf{Ans} type is deliberately left abstract and can be instantiated with different types, enabling the semantics to serve different purposes.

The semantics function 𝔼​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{E}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket is recursively defined over the input list of instructions. Given a list of instructions e​ses, 𝔼​⟦𝑒𝑠⟧\mathbb{E}\llbracket~\mathit{es}~\rrbracket returns a function taking a stack, environment, continuation, and a trail, and produces 𝖠𝗇𝗌\mathsf{Ans}. If the list is empty, we simply invoke the continuation. If the list is not empty, we pattern-match on the first instruction and define its semantics accordingly, and recursively call 𝔼​⟦𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑡⟧\mathbb{E}\llbracket~\mathit{rest}~\rrbracket when necessary. The trail is represented as a list of continuations and serves as a table, modeling block jumps local to a function, which we will explain later with control flow.

In our semantics, we pass the updated state explicitly to recursive calls to 𝔼​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{E}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket or continuations rather than updating them in place. The 𝗇𝗈𝗉\mathsf{nop} instruction leaves the state unchanged, while 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍​c\mathsf{const}~c pushes cc onto the stack. 𝗅𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅.𝗀𝖾𝗍​x\mathsf{local.get}~x loads the value at index xx in the environment onto the stack, while 𝗅𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗅.𝗌𝖾𝗍​x\mathsf{local.set}~x pops the stack and writes the popped value at index xx in the environment. For brevity, several rules pattern-match on the stack. For example, the t.𝖺𝖽𝖽t.\mathsf{add} rule matches v1::v2::σv_{1}::v_{2}::\sigma, where v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} are the top two stack values and σ\sigma is the remainder. We write σ1m++σ2\sigma_{1}\prescript{}{m}{+}\mkern-13.0mu+\sigma_{2} for a stack split into a top segment σ1\sigma_{1} of length mm and a remainder σ2\sigma_{2}, and ⌊σ⌋n\left\lfloor\sigma\right\rfloor_{n} for the top nn values of σ\sigma.

Control Flow

Now we go through several control-flow instructions to illustrate how continuations and trail are used. The control-flow instructions 𝖻𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄\mathsf{block}, 𝗅𝗈𝗈𝗉\mathsf{loop}, and 𝗂𝖿\mathsf{if} add a new continuation to the control context θ\theta, which defines the behavior of branching instruction 𝖻𝗋\mathsf{br}. The 𝖻𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄\mathsf{block} instruction evaluates the body instructions e​ses with an updated control context that adds a new continuation κ1\kappa_{1} to the trail θ\theta. The continuation κ1\kappa_{1} captures the control flow after the block.

To enter this continuation via 𝖻𝗋​l\mathsf{br}~l instruction, we look up the ll-th continuation in the trail θ\theta, and the control flow will jump to the corresponding continuation. On the right, the first 𝖻𝗋​0\mathsf{br}~0 jumps to the end of the innermost block, which is captured by the continuation at the top of the trail within the scope of the block. The 𝗅𝗈𝗈𝗉\mathsf{loop} instruction is similar to 𝖻𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄\mathsf{block}, but the continuation κ2\kappa_{2} added to the trail θ\theta will re-evaluate the loop body e​ses when branched to via 𝖻𝗋​l\mathsf{br}~l. This is exemplified by the 𝖻𝗋​0\mathsf{br}~0 at the end of the example. The 𝗂𝖿\mathsf{if} instruction first pops the value vv from the stack. Then when vv is not zero, it recursively evaluates the instructions e​s1es_{1} with the continuation κ1\kappa_{1} pushes onto trail θ\theta, where κ1\kappa_{1} captures the control flow after the true branch. Otherwise it evaluates e​s2es_{2} in the false-branch with the same control context.

Function Call and Return

The 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅​x\mathsf{call}~x instruction retrieves xx’s definition using 𝗅𝗈𝗈𝗄𝗎𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇𝖼\mathsf{lookupFunc} and uses 𝖻𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖤𝗇𝗏\mathsf{buildEnv} to construct ρ1\rho_{1} from the argument list σ𝑎𝑟𝑔\sigma_{\mathit{arg}}, allocating extra space for local variables. Finally, the 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅​x\mathsf{call}~x instruction evaluates the function body e​ses under an empty stack, ρ1\rho_{1} and a control context initialized with continuation κ1\kappa_{1}. This control context corresponds to the target function’s scope and is a singleton list containing κ1\kappa_{1}, which captures the control flow after the function call. In the function body, the 𝗋𝖾𝗍𝗎𝗋𝗇\mathsf{return} instruction invokes the last trail continuation κ1\kappa_{1}, skipping all enclosing blocks. Readers can refer to (Wei et al., 2025) for more details on Wasm’s CPS semantics.

3. Concolic Execution with Continuations

The concrete CPS semantics of μ\muWasm (Section 2.3) forms the basis for developing our compositional concolic execution semantics, which we present in this section. When presenting formalization, we highlight the symbolic extensions relative to the concrete semantics.

3.1. Concrete-Input-Controlled Symbolic Execution

We first extend the semantic domains with symbolic counterparts and then define the concolic semantics as a definitional interpreter ℂ​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket. The new symbolic components collect path conditions during execution without affecting the program’s concrete behavior, so the concolic semantics subsumes the concrete one. At the same time, it remains compositional and uses continuations to make control flow explicit.

Symbolic Semantic Domains

Figure 4 highlights the extended semantic domains. 𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼\mathsf{Symbolic} values ss are a superset of concrete values vv, additionally including symbols 𝖲𝗒𝗆⁡(x)\mathsf{Sym}(x) identified by xx, and unary (o​p1#​s1op^{\#}_{1}~s_{1}) and binary (s1​o​p2#​s2s_{1}~op^{\#}_{2}~s_{2}) symbolic expressions.

We use a single stack and environment to store both concrete and symbolic values. Thus, the symbolic stack 𝖲𝗍𝖺𝖼𝗄#\mathsf{Stack}^{\#} and environment 𝖤𝗇𝗏#\mathsf{Env}^{\#} are lists of pairs ⟨v,s⟩\langle v,s\rangle, where vv is a concrete value and ss is its corresponding symbolic expression under the current path condition. Path conditions 𝖯𝖢\mathsf{PC} are represented as lists of symbolic values, with newly encountered conditions pushed to the front. The conjunction of all expressions in 𝖯𝖢\mathsf{PC} is the constraints on symbolic inputs to trigger the current execution path. Finally, continuation functions 𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍#\mathsf{Cont}^{\#} take a concolic stack, environment, and path conditions as input. The return type 𝖠𝗇𝗌\mathsf{Ans} is left polymorphic to allow different instantiations.

Definitional Concolic Interpreter

Figure 4 shows an excerpt of the concolic semantics as a definitional interpreter. Compared to the concrete semantics (Figure 3), the concolic semantics ℂ​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket is extended to take path conditions π#\pi^{\#} as additional inputs, and other components are lifted to their concolic counterparts. Most of the changes to the interpreter are structural: the control flow is unchanged and we simply pass around the symbolic components, therefore the cases for 𝑛𝑖𝑙\mathit{nil}, block, loop, call, and return are omitted and can be found in Appendix A.

We explain concolic execution through representative cases. The symbolic interpretation of numeric operations mirrors their concrete construction. For example, t.𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍​ct.\mathsf{const}~c creates a concrete–symbolic pair ⟨c,c⟩\langle c,c\rangle and pushes it onto the concolic stack, while t.𝖺𝖽𝖽t.\mathsf{add} builds the corresponding symbolic addition expression. We collect path conditions when encountering conditional instructions. In the ℂ​⟦𝗂𝖿​…⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\mathsf{if}\dots~\rrbracket case, we first pop the concolic condition ⟨v,s⟩\langle v,s\rangle from the stack. The concrete value vv determines the branch to take, as in the concrete semantics, while the symbolic value ss updates the path condition: depending on the branch, ss or ¬s\neg s is prepended to π#\pi^{\#}, yielding a new path condition π1#\pi^{\#}_{1} that is passed to the evaluation of the chosen branch.

Initial Continuation

To invoke the concolic definitional interpreter, we provide the initial halting continuation κh​a​l​t#\kappa^{\#}_{halt}. The interpreter’s return type 𝖠𝗇𝗌\mathsf{Ans} is polymorphic over different instantiations of this continuation. For concolic execution, we instantiate it to return the collected path conditions upon completion κh​a​l​t#​(_,_,π#)=π#\kappa^{\#}_{halt}(\_,\_,\pi^{\#})=\pi^{\#}. The concolic execution scheduler (described below) uses the returned path conditions to generate new inputs and explore alternative paths.

3.2. Concolic Execution Scheduler

Given an input Wasm program, the concolic scheduler (Algorithm 1) orchestrates the exploration of paths by invoking ℂ​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket with varying inputs that lead to distinct paths. The scheduler takes as input a module, the entry function name ff, and a list of initial arguments, which may include both symbolic (i.e., 𝖲𝗒𝗆⁡(x)\mathsf{Sym}(x)) and concrete values. It maintains a worklist 𝑊𝐿∈𝒫⁡(𝖯𝖢#)\mathit{WL}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{PC^{\#}}) of path conditions to explore, where 𝒫⁡(⋅)\mathcal{P}(\cdot) is the powerset operator. Each path condition represents constraints on symbolic inputs leading to an unexplored path if satisfied. Initially, the worklist contains only the empty path condition, since no paths have yet been explored and any input is valid.

In each iteration, the scheduler pops a path condition 𝑝𝑐\mathit{pc} from the worklist and invokes an SMT solver to find a satisfying assignment. We model the solver as a function 𝑠𝑜𝑙𝑣𝑒:𝖯𝖢→𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅∪𝖴𝖭𝖲𝖠𝖳\mathit{solve}:\mathsf{PC}\to\mathsf{Model}\cup{\mathsf{UNSAT}}, where a model is a partial mapping from symbolic variables to concrete values:

m∈𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅=𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖵𝖺𝗋⇀𝖵𝖺𝗅𝗎𝖾.m\in\mathsf{Model}=\mathsf{SymVar}\rightharpoonup\mathsf{Value}.

If 𝑝𝑐\mathit{pc} is unsatisfiable, the scheduler skips the path as there is no possible input to reach this path. Otherwise, to construct the initial concolic input stack for executing ℂ​⟦𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅​f⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\mathsf{call}~f~\rrbracket, we use an auxiliary function 𝑖𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑡𝑒:(𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼],𝖬𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗅)→𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖵𝖺𝗅𝗎𝖾×𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼]\mathit{instantiate}:(\mathsf{List[Symbolic]},\mathsf{Model})\to\mathsf{List[Value\times Symbolic]} that evaluates each symbolic input under the model and pairs the resulting concrete value with the original symbolic input. The scheduler then invokes ℂ​⟦𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅​f⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\mathsf{call}~f~\rrbracket with the constructed concolic stack, empty environment, initial continuation trail [κh​a​l​t#][\kappa^{\#}_{halt}], and halting continuation κh​a​l​t#\kappa^{\#}_{halt} to explore a new path.

Upon completion, the interpreter returns the collected path condition π1\pi_{1}. The scheduler then generates new path conditions by negating each constraint in π1\pi_{1}, as detailed in Appendix A, adds the resulting conditions to the worklist, and proceeds to the next iteration. When the worklist becomes empty, all feasible execution paths have been covered.

4. Compiling Concolic Execution with Continuations

The concolic semantics developed in Section 3 can already be implemented as a definitional interpreter. Although conceptually straightforward, this interpreter incurs significant overhead from repeatedly dispatching on instructions, which can greatly impact performance (Wiedmann, 1983; Lion et al., 2022; Würthinger et al., 2017). In this section, we build a concolic-execution compiler to eliminate this overhead by realizing the first Futamura projection (Futamura, 1999; Futamura, 1971) through multi-stage programming (MSP) (Taha, 1999). We refactor the concolic semantics into a compiler that generates efficient concolic execution code without interpretation overhead. Section 4.1 briefly introduces MSP and the notations used later, and Section 4.2 presents the staged concolic semantics for μ\muWasm.

4.1. A Brief Overview of Multi-Stage Programming

Multi-stage programming is a generative programming paradigm that enables programs to construct and manipulate other programs. By dividing computation into multiple stages, programmers annotate code to indicate which parts depend on static input known at earlier stages and which depend on dynamic input available only later. The resulting residual program contains only computations that depend on dynamic input, while computations over static input have been performed in earlier stages. Writing an interpreter in an MSP language allows us to specialize it to the static program representation, effectively achieving programmer-guided partial evaluation (Jones et al., 1993).

Later, in Section 4.2, we specify the staged concolic semantics using the quasi-quotation and splicing syntax from Scala 3 (Stucki et al., 2021). A quotation '​{e}\texttt{\textquotesingle}\{\,e\,\} (or simply '​e\texttt{\textquotesingle}e) denotes a next-stage expression ee, while splicing '​{…​$​{e}​…}\texttt{\textquotesingle}\{\,\dots\texttt{\$}\{\,e\,\}\dots\,\} inserts the value of a current-stage expression ee into the surrounding quotation. At the type level, 𝖤𝗑𝗉𝗋⁡[𝖳]\mathsf{\mathsf{Expr}[T]} represents a next-stage type TT.

Figure 5 illustrates MSP with the power function example. The single-stage function 𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{power} computes xnx^{n} recursively. When the exponent nn is known in advance, we can write a multi-stage version 𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{genpower}, which generates a specialized 𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{power} function taking only xx as input. In 𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{genpower}, the variable xx is marked as a next-stage value by type 𝖤𝗑𝗉𝗋⁡[𝖨𝗇𝗍]\mathsf{Expr}[\mathsf{Int}], and the result is a next-stage expression that computes xnx^{n}. When n=0n=0, 𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{genpower} produces the staged constant '​1\texttt{\textquotesingle}1; when n>0n>0, it constructs a staged expression multiplying xx by the result of a recursive call with n−1n-1.

By providing a concrete value for the static input nn, we can specialize 𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{genpower} and produce a residual program that depends only on xx. For instance, we specialize 𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{genpower} to obtain power2\mathit{power2} by applying 𝗋𝗎𝗇\mathsf{run}, a common construct for evaluating staged expressions in MSP languages (Stucki et al., 2021; Kiselyov, 2014; Taha and Sheard, 1997). Compared to the generic 𝑝𝑜𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{power} function, power2\mathit{power2} for n=2n=2 unrolls all recursive calls and eliminates the overhead of condition checks.

4.2. Compilation of Concolic Semantics

We now develop the staged concolic semantics 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket for μ\muWasm. Specializing 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket to a source program generates efficient concolic execution code and realizes the first Futamura projection (Futamura, 1999; Futamura, 1971). Since the unstaged semantics ℂ​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket (Figure 4) is compositional (Jones, 1996), we derive 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket in Figure 7 by adding stage annotations to ℂ​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket without altering the concolic evaluation logic. During specialization, the staged semantics mostly unrolls recursive calls over subterms.

In the presentation of staged semantics, variables bound to current stage values are orange, while those bound to staged expressions are blue. We do not add any color for variables at next stage.

Staging Semantic Domains

The domains of the staged semantics are derived from the concolic semantics (Figure 4) by analyzing whether values in each domain depend on the static program or dynamic input. If they depend on dynamic input, we lift their type to the second stage by wrapping it in 𝖤𝗑𝗉𝗋\mathsf{Expr}. The stack, environment, and path condition contain runtime values, so we lift their types to the second stage. Since the generated code invokes continuations with these runtime states, continuations are also lifted. The trail is a list of continuations, but only the continuations within the list are residualized:

θ#\displaystyle\theta^{\#} ∈𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗂𝗅#\displaystyle\in\mathsf{Trail^{\#}} =𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖤𝗑𝗉𝗋⁡[𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍#]]\displaystyle=\mathchoice{\hbox{\pagecolor{teal!12}$\displaystyle\mathsf{List[\mathsf{Expr}[Cont^{\#}]]}$}}{\hbox{\pagecolor{teal!12}$\textstyle\mathsf{List[\mathsf{Expr}[Cont^{\#}]]}$}}{\hbox{\pagecolor{teal!12}$\scriptstyle\mathsf{List[\mathsf{Expr}[Cont^{\#}]]}$}}{\hbox{\pagecolor{teal!12}$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{List[\mathsf{Expr}[Cont^{\#}]]}$}}

A careful (manual) binding-time analysis of the concolic semantics shows that the static source-program structure and control flow, such as 𝖻𝗋​i\mathsf{br}~i, completely determine the trail structure and its access indices at compile time. Because its structure is known statically, the list remains a current-stage value and need not be lifted to 𝖤𝗑𝗉𝗋⁡[𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍#]]\mathsf{Expr[List[Cont^{\#}]]}.

Compiling Mutually Recursive Functions

Since WebAssembly function definitions can be mutually recursive, directly unrolling recursive calls could lead to non-terminating specialization. To ensure termination in the staged semantics, we introduce a run-time construct 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo} that memoizes compiled Wasm function definitions. Instead of unrolling calls, we generate code that, at runtime, looks up the callee’s compiled function in 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo} and invokes it.

𝑚𝑒𝑚𝑜∈𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\displaystyle\mathit{memo}\in\mathsf{Memo} =𝖬𝖺𝗉[𝖨𝖽𝖾𝗇𝗍𝗂𝖿𝗂𝖾𝗋,(𝖤𝗇𝗏#,𝖯𝖢#,𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍#,𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈)→𝖠𝗇𝗌]\displaystyle=\mathsf{Map}[\mathsf{Identifier},(\mathsf{Env^{\#}},\mathsf{PC^{\#}},\mathsf{Cont^{\#}},\mathsf{Memo})\rightarrow\mathsf{Ans}]

We define a module semantics 𝕄​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{M}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket (Figure 6) that traverses all functions in a Wasm module only once and produces the 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo} with their staged function definitions. 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo} is self-referential: the functions in 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo} access the 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo} itself to call to other functions. When later interpreting a 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅\mathsf{call} instruction, we generate code looking up the corresponding compiled function in the memo. In practice, we implement staging with LMS (Rompf and Odersky, 2010), which internally memoizes staged function definitions, so recursive references reuse an existing definition rather than recompile its body. This prevents recursive calls from causing non-terminating specialization and eliminates the need to maintain 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo} explicitly.

Adding Stage Annotations to Concolic Semantics

Now, we can refactor the concolic semantics into its staged version. The staging annotations indicate the evaluation time of expressions, staged expressions marked with '​{⋅}\texttt{\textquotesingle}\{\,\cdot\,\} are delayed to runtime, while those unmarked are evaluated during specialization. Compared to the concolic semantics ℂ​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket, we replace the pattern matching on the stack σ#\sigma^{\#} with explicit stack manipulation operations 𝗁𝖾𝖺𝖽\mathsf{head} and 𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗅\mathsf{tail} for clarity. 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket does not evaluate the final result of the program, instead, it constructs next-stage expressions that compute the final result when executed. In the following, we explain a few representative cases.

  • •

    In the case of t.𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍​ct.\mathsf{const}~{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}c}, we splice the current stack σ#\sigma^{\#} into a staged expression that constructs the new stack. Then, we call 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket recursively with the staged new stack to build the expression that computes the final result. Since c{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}c} is a current stage value, we call meta-function 𝗅𝗂𝖿𝗍\mathsf{lift} to convert it to a next stage value before using it in the staged expression.

  • •

    For blocks, 𝕊​⟦𝖻𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄​…⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\mathsf{block}\dots~\rrbracket produces a staged let-expression that defines the continuation κ1#\kappa^{\#}_{1} and splices the result of applying 𝕊​⟦e​s⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}es}~\rrbracket to the block body.

    We define continuation κ1#\kappa^{\#}_{1} by splicing the call of 𝕊​⟦r​e​s​t⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}rest}~\rrbracket. The continuation κ1#\kappa^{\#}_{1} maintains a valid stack matching the return type of this 𝖻𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄\mathsf{block} when calling 𝕊​⟦r​e​s​t⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}rest}~\rrbracket: κ1#\kappa^{\#}_{1} first truncates the top nn elements from the incoming stack σ1#\sigma^{\#}_{1} and appends the remaining stack σ#{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}\sigma^{\#}} after dropping its top mm elements. When invoked, κ1#\kappa^{\#}_{1} receives the latest environment ρ1#\rho^{\#}_{1} and path condition π1#\pi^{\#}_{1}. Since ρ1#\rho^{\#}_{1} and π1#\pi^{\#}_{1} are variables bound by a staged λ\lambda-term, we quote them when referencing them in the spliced expression.

    Finally, to generate code computing the 𝖻𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄\mathsf{block} result, we call 𝕊​⟦e​s⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}es}~\rrbracket on the block body using the top mm elements of the stack σ#{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}\sigma^{\#}}, the continuation '​κ1#\texttt{\textquotesingle}\kappa^{\#}_{1}, and the trail '​κ1#::θ#\texttt{\textquotesingle}\kappa^{\#}_{1}::{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}\theta^{\#}}.

  • •

    The 𝗅𝗈𝗈𝗉\mathsf{loop} case is similar to 𝖻𝗅𝗈𝖼𝗄\mathsf{block}, except that we additionally construct a staged continuation κ2#\kappa^{\#}_{2} representing the start of the loop body. Invoking κ2#\kappa^{\#}_{2} with the current stack, environment, and path conditions produces the final result of this case.

  • •

    For the 𝗂𝖿\mathsf{if} instruction, we first pop the condition ⟨v,s⟩\langle v,s\rangle from the stack and prepare the block arguments by taking the top mm items from the remaining stack. The remaining computation after the 𝗂𝖿\mathsf{if} is residualized into continuation κ1#\kappa^{\#}_{1}. We build a new path condition π1#\pi^{\#}_{1} by prepending ss for the true branch and ¬s\neg s for the false branch to the current path condition π#\pi^{\#}.

    Finally, we generate a staged conditional expression whose branches splice the current-stage calls 𝕊​⟦e​s1⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}es_{1}}~\rrbracket and 𝕊​⟦e​s2⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~{\color[rgb]{1,0.23,0.13}es_{2}}~\rrbracket, respectively. We quote '​σ𝑎𝑟𝑔#\texttt{\textquotesingle}\sigma^{\#}_{\mathit{arg}}, '​π1#\texttt{\textquotesingle}\pi^{\#}_{1}, and '​κ1#\texttt{\textquotesingle}\kappa^{\#}_{1} when passing them to 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket, since these variables are created inside the staged expression, while we pass ρ#{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}\rho^{\#}} directly because it is a current-stage variable bound to a staged expression.

  • •

    In the case of 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅\mathsf{call}, we first retrieve the function identifier using the compile-time function 𝗅𝗈𝗈𝗄𝗎𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇𝖼\mathsf{lookupFunc}. With the identifier xx, we look up the run-time 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo}-table 𝑚𝑒𝑚𝑜\mathit{memo} to retrieve the compiled function ff. We prepare the argument environment ρ1#\rho^{\#}_{1} and continuation κ1#\kappa^{\#}_{1}, similar to the unstaged counterpart. Finally, we generate a runtime call to ff with the prepared arguments.

A Working Example

Figure 8(a) shows a Wasm block that computes the maximum of two integers stored in local variables using an 𝗂𝖿\mathsf{if} instruction. Its compiled concolic execution, obtained by applying the staged concolic semantics 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket, is shown in Figure 8(b). Since the dispatching on the instructions has been performed during the staging, the specialized program contains only the computations necessary to compute the maximum of two integers and build the path conditions. The administrative instructions such as stack resizing and pushing/popping frames have been compiled away. In other words, the interpretation overhead has been eliminated.

4.3. Staged Concolic Scheduler

We adapt the exploration scheduler to work with the compiled concolic program and show it in Appendix A. The scheduler is a runtime function that invokes the staged module semantics 𝕄​⟦𝑚𝑜𝑑⟧\mathbb{M}\llbracket~\mathit{mod}~\rrbracket to compile all Wasm functions. Then, using MSP’s standard facility 𝗋𝗎𝗇\mathsf{run}, the scheduler evaluates the generated staged expression to obtain a map of compiled functions.

The compiled program executes only the essential concolic logic for the source program, eliminating interpretation overhead from instruction dispatching. In practice, the scheduler can be implemented in the same language as the generated program and invoke the compiled code directly. For example, in GenWasym implementation (Section 7), we generate C++ code for concolic execution of Wasm programs, and the scheduler is also implemented in C++ as part of the runtime, which will be linked with the generated code.

4.4. Termination and Correctness of Compilation

Since we are building a compiler, we must ensure that our staging process terminates and produces staged programs that preserve the source semantics. The staged concolic interpreter 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket avoids diverging for recursive Wasm function calls by using the 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo} to store staged function definitions. We construct a staged function call by looking up its definition from 𝖬𝖾𝗆𝗈\mathsf{Memo}, rather than directly evaluating (i.e., specializing) the function’s body.

Compared to building a concolic-compiler from scratch, our approach is not only simpler but also easier to reason about its correctness, since the unstaged interpretation serves as the specification:

∀𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡,𝑓𝑠,𝑒𝑠.𝗋𝗎𝗇⁡(𝕊⁡⟦𝑒𝑠⟧​(𝕄⁡⟦𝑓𝑠⟧))​(𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡,ρ0#,π0#,κhalt,[κhalt])≡ℂ⁡⟦𝑒𝑠⟧​(𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡,ρ0#,π0#,κhalt,[κhalt])\forall\mathit{input},\mathit{fs},\mathit{es}.\mathsf{run}(\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\mathit{es}~\rrbracket(\mathbb{M}\llbracket~\mathit{fs}~\rrbracket))(\mathit{input},\rho^{\#}_{0},\pi^{\#}_{0},\kappa_{\text{halt}},[\kappa_{\text{halt}}])\equiv\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\mathit{es}~\rrbracket(\mathit{input},\rho^{\#}_{0},\pi^{\#}_{0},\kappa_{\text{halt}},[\kappa_{\text{halt}}])

The equation states that the staging semantics 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket and 𝕄​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{M}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket must agree with the original concolic semantics ℂ​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket. This property requires the source program and the specialized program always return the same result when given the same 𝑖𝑛𝑝𝑢𝑡\mathit{input} and other initial arguments, including empty environment ρ0#\rho^{\#}_{0}, empty path condition π0#\pi^{\#}_{0}, halt continuation κhalt\kappa_{\text{halt}}, and trail with only κhalt\kappa_{\text{halt}}. The specialized program is obtained by applying 𝗋𝗎𝗇\mathsf{run} on the staged term produced by 𝕊​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{S}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket and 𝕄​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{M}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket. On the right-hand side of the equation, ℂ​⟦⋅⟧\mathbb{C}\llbracket~\cdot~\rrbracket does not take 𝑓𝑠\mathit{fs} as input, because it implicitly accesses function definitions in the module via 𝗅𝗈𝗈𝗄𝗎𝗉𝖥𝗎𝗇𝖼\mathsf{lookupFunc}.

5. Snapshotting Compiled Concolic Execution with Continuations

The scheduler defined in Section 4.3 re-executes the program from the beginning for each new input, causing redundant work along shared path prefixes. This redundancy becomes costly for programs with deep execution paths. We now present the snapshot-reuse optimization, which uses continuations to eliminate redundant execution in the compiled concolic program and its scheduler.

Conceptually, concolic execution explores an implicit execution tree whose nodes represent branch points, leaves mark execution ends, and root-to-leaf paths correspond to complete traces. As the tree expands, both the number of leaves and the re-execution cost grow exponentially. The key idea is to save both program states and continuations at branch points, which together we call snapshots. Resuming from snapshots explores new paths instead of re-executing shared path segments.

From State-Passing to Global Mutable States

Resuming from a snapshot requires symbolic states sufficient to reconstruct the entire program state. However, the staging semantics in Figure 7 works on a local stack and environment that are passed as parameters. These parameters capture only a portion of the program state rather than the entire state. For example, in Figure 7, we always ensure the function’s local stack is initialized to empty before entering the function body, hence the caller’s stack is not visible to the callee. Therefore, we refactor the state-passing interpreter to use mutable global variables, i.e., σg#{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}\sigma_{g}^{\#}}, ρg#{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}\rho_{g}^{\#}}, and πg#{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}\pi_{g}^{\#}}, which hold references to the entire stack, environment, and path condition, respectively. Accordingly, the continuation function type does not take any argument and performs effects by updating these globals: κ#∈𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍#=()→𝖠𝗇𝗌\kappa^{\#}\in\mathsf{Cont^{\#}}=()\to\mathsf{Ans}.

Capturing Snapshots

A snapshot is a triple consisting of continuations, symbolic stacks, and symbolic environments. Together they capture necessary information to resume execution from a branch point. We also redefine 𝖯𝖢#\mathsf{PC^{\#}} to include snapshots of the untaken branch in addition to the constraints of the taken branch:

Σ∈𝖲𝗇𝖺𝗉𝗌𝗁𝗈𝗍\displaystyle\Sigma\in\mathsf{Snapshot} =𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍#×𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼]×𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼]\displaystyle=\mathsf{Cont^{\#}}\times\mathsf{List[Symbolic]}\times\mathsf{List[Symbolic]}
π#∈𝖯𝖢#\displaystyle\pi^{\#}\in\mathsf{PC^{\#}} =𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼×𝖲𝗇𝖺𝗉𝗌𝗁𝗈𝗍].\displaystyle=\mathsf{List[Symbolic\times\mathsf{Snapshot}]}.

Figure 9 highlights the modification to the staged semantics in Figure 7 for handling 𝗂𝖿\mathsf{if} instructions. The key change is to represent the computations of the “then” and “else” branches as next-stage continuations, κ𝑡𝑟𝑢#\kappa^{\#}_{\mathit{tru}} and κ𝑓𝑙𝑠#\kappa^{\#}_{\mathit{fls}}. Using these continuations and the current symbolic states, we create the corresponding snapshots Σ𝑡𝑟𝑢\Sigma_{\mathit{tru}} and Σ𝑓𝑙𝑠\Sigma_{\mathit{fls}}. Since the stack consists of concolic pairs, we extract the symbolic stack using σ#.𝗌𝗒𝗆\sigma^{\#}.\mathsf{sym}, and apply the same to the environment. We then update the global path condition according to the branch taken and invoke the corresponding continuation.

Since now the symbolic stack/environment are global mutable states, operations on them also become imperative. At the beginning, we pop the concolic condition from the global stack σ#{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}\sigma^{\#}} by 𝗉𝗈𝗉!\mathsf{pop}^{!}. We mark these effectful operations on global states with a superscript exclamation mark. Recall that in WebAssembly, the type of 𝗂𝖿\mathsf{if} regulates the input/output stack: the branches can access top mm elements on the stack, and each branch leaves the stack with nn new elements after removing the mm inputs. Therefore, we save the stack below those mm inputs into σ𝑜𝑙𝑑#\sigma^{\#}_{\mathit{old}}. When resuming via κ1#\kappa^{\#}_{1}, we use the result of prepending the nn outputs to σ𝑜𝑙𝑑#\sigma^{\#}_{\mathit{old}} to restore the global stack σg#{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}\sigma_{g}^{\#}}.

Resuming from Snapshots

Algorithm 2 shows a modified scheduler that reconstructs concrete states from snapshots to resume the execution without re-executing from the beginning.

The worklist pairs path conditions and their corresponding snapshots. It is initialized with an empty path condition and a snapshot of the program entry. In each iteration, the scheduler pops a pair and checks the condition’s feasibility as in Section 3. If the condition is satisfiable, it uses the model to instantiate the snapshot’s symbolic states to update the global states. The scheduler then invokes the continuation stored in the snapshot to resume execution from the branch point. The execution returns a new Π#\Pi^{\#} pairing taken-branch path conditions with snapshots of the untaken branches. Finally, the scheduler calls Negate to append the untaken branches’ path conditions and snapshots to the worklist for future exploration. Thus, continuation-based resumption avoids re-executing shared path prefixes while retaining the performance of compiled execution.

Improving Asymptotic Complexity

By applying snapshots to avoid re-execution, we improve the asymptotic complexity of concolic execution. Suppose the implicit execution tree of a concolic execution contains nn nodes. The tree’s height ranges from O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) (balanced) to O⁡(n)O(n) (unbalanced). The complexity of exploring a path from root to leaf takes between O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) and O⁡(n)O(n), and exploring all paths from the root takes between O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) to O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}). With snapshots, however, each exploration starts from a fresh node that has never been visited before. As a result, every node is visited exactly once, reducing the overall complexity to O⁡(n)O(n) in the worst case.

6. Deciding When to Use Snapshots

Section 5 introduced snapshots to uniformly avoid re-executing previously explored program prefixes. Its practical effectiveness, however, depends on both the depth of the shared execution prefix and the size of the resumed symbolic state. For programs whose execution paths share only shallow prefixes, creating and instantiating snapshots may cost more than re-executing the program. Thus, applying snapshot reuse uniformly, as in Algorithm 2, may yield little benefit or even degrade performance for such programs.

The figure on the right illustrates this trade-off for the quicksort benchmark used in our evaluation (Section 8.2). The benchmark contains 862 complete paths and 861 branch points. Each of the 861 plotted points represents the choice at one branch point between resuming from its snapshot and re-executing from the program entry to reach it. The x-axis shows the re-execution cost and the y-axis the snapshot-resumption cost. Of these 861 choices, 283 lie above the dashed equal-cost line, indicating that snapshot resumption is more expensive than re-execution. In this example, reusing snapshots uniformly at these unprofitable points would therefore make the overall execution slower than uniform re-execution, as the overall cost of these 283 snapshots is substantially higher than the cost of re-execution.

Additionally, the snapshot mechanism in Figure 9 captures only the states represented in the semantics. However, realistic programs interact with external environments (e.g., the OS), whose states are typically not preserved in a snapshot. When an execution path involves such interactions, the symbolic state recorded in the snapshot may no longer be reachable in a concrete execution. In that case, resuming from the snapshot may break the soundness of concolic execution.

To make snapshot reuse both effective and sound, we need a strategy for deciding when to resume execution from a snapshot and when re-execution from the beginning is preferable. This section develops a heuristic for making this choice based on cost estimation while enforcing soundness.

Cost of Re-execution vs. Instantiation

The main cost of instantiating a snapshot comes from reconstructing the concrete state from the snapshot, which involves traversing all symbolic expressions in the symbolic stack and environment and evaluating them with respect to the SMT model. We estimate this cost by the number of symbolic expressions and denote it as CInsC_{\text{Ins}}:

CIns\displaystyle C_{\text{Ins}} =δ∗(𝗌𝗂𝗓𝖾𝖮𝖿𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖤𝗑𝗉⁡(σ#)+𝗌𝗂𝗓𝖾𝖮𝖿𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖤𝗑𝗉⁡(ρ#))\displaystyle=\delta*(\mathsf{sizeOfSymExp}(\sigma^{\#})+\mathsf{sizeOfSymExp}(\rho^{\#}))

where parameter δ\delta is the average timing cost of evaluating symbolic expressions in the solver. In practice, we can obtain δ\delta by measuring the evaluation time of a large set of symbolic expressions. During runtime, we also record the execution time from the beginning of the program to the branch point as the re-execution cost, denoted CReC_{\text{Re}}.

Soundly Handling External Calls

External calls invoke functions whose implementations are unavailable to the concolic or symbolic execution engine, such as system calls or library calls. One way to handle external calls is to execute them concretely and treat the returned concrete values as their symbolic counterparts in subsequent concolic execution.

However, this strategy can make snapshot reuse unsound: a snapshot based on an observed concrete return value assumes that the external call returns the same value across executions. In a fresh execution from the beginning, the call may return a different value because its arguments or the external environment have changed. As a result, the symbolic states captured by the snapshot may be invalid, and the resumed execution may fail to correspond to a feasible program path.

To avoid creating unsound snapshots, we can conservatively disable resumption of snapshots whose execution prefix contains an external call. For such snapshots, instead of computing CInsC_{\text{Ins}} using 𝗌𝗂𝗓𝖾𝖮𝖿𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖤𝗑𝗉\mathsf{sizeOfSymExp}, we set it to infinity, ensuring that the scheduler re-executes the program from beginning. A more sophisticated concolic execution engine can handle external calls soundly by symbolically modeling the semantics of external functions. We leave the integration of sound external call handling and its interaction with snapshot reuse as future work.

Heuristic Decision

The decision of whether to resume from a snapshot at a branch therefore reduces to comparing the cost of instantiation with that of re-execution. At runtime, we compute the ratio CRe/CInsC_{\text{Re}}/C_{\text{Ins}}. If this ratio exceeds 1, re-execution is deemed more expensive than instantiation, and we therefore prefer to resume from the snapshot. Otherwise, we re-execute the program from the beginning. To implement this heuristic, we extend 𝖲𝗇𝖺𝗉𝗌𝗁𝗈𝗍\mathsf{Snapshot} with an additional field 𝖢𝗈𝗌𝗍\mathsf{Cost} = 𝖨𝗇𝗍\mathsf{Int}, which estimates the cost of reaching the program point at which the snapshot was created:

s∈𝖲𝗇𝖺𝗉𝗌𝗁𝗈𝗍=𝖢𝗈𝗇𝗍#×𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼]×𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍⁡[𝖲𝗒𝗆𝖻𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼]×𝖢𝗈𝗌𝗍.s\in\mathsf{Snapshot}=\mathsf{Cont^{\#}}\times\mathsf{List[Symbolic]}\times\mathsf{List[Symbolic]}\times\mathchoice{\hbox{\pagecolor{teal!12}$\displaystyle\mathsf{Cost}$}}{\hbox{\pagecolor{teal!12}$\textstyle\mathsf{Cost}$}}{\hbox{\pagecolor{teal!12}$\scriptstyle\mathsf{Cost}$}}{\hbox{\pagecolor{teal!12}$\scriptscriptstyle\mathsf{Cost}$}}.

Appendix A presents the heuristic scheduler. In each iteration, the scheduler compares the cost stored in the snapshot against the estimated cost of instantiation, represented by the size of the symbolic state.

7. Implementation

We scale our approach to a substantially larger subset of WebAssembly and implement it in GenWasym, a compiler written in Scala using the Lightweight Modular Staging (LMS) framework (Rompf and Odersky, 2010).

7.1. Compilation via Staging

At the core of GenWasym is a staged concolic interpreter for WebAssembly, derived from our staged concolic semantics with snapshots. Compilation is performed by specializing this interpreter to a given Wasm program. Unlike the quasi-quotation and splicing presentations in earlier sections, the implementation uses LMS (Rompf and Odersky, 2010), which offers convenient staging APIs through operator overloading. As a result, while the implementation follows the same staging semantics and type-level stage discipline, it does not use explicit quasi-quotation/splicing syntax. LMS also provides a graph-based IR with built-in optimizations (Bracevac et al., 2023), as well as multiple code-generation backends, including C++. The core staged interpreter of GenWasym comprises 1.5K lines of Scala code.

GenWasym generates efficient C++ code for concolic execution in CPS. Each WebAssembly function is compiled into a C++ function that takes an additional continuation argument. Following the refactoring described in Section 5, the stack, environment, and path condition are maintained as global mutable runtime states, and the generated code operates directly on them. Continuations therefore do not need to thread these states explicitly. Moreover, the continuation trail disappears entirely in the generated code, since all computation over the trail is resolved at the first stage (Section 4). WebAssembly stack and frame operations compile directly to operations on the corresponding global runtime structures. To support efficient state snapshotting, we represent the stack and environment using persistent data structures from Immer (Puente, 2017), which provide efficient copy and update operations while reducing the need to copy large amounts of memory.

7.2. Supporting More WebAssembly Features

GenWasym supports all numeric types in Wasm 2.0 (Rossberg, 2022), including 32-/64-bit integers and floating-point numbers. Symbolically, these values are represented using the bit-vector and floating-point theories of Z3 (de Moura and Bjørner, 2008). Beyond the features covered in our core formalization, GenWasym supports a large fragment of commonly used WebAssembly features, including additional arithmetic operations, function tables, indirect calls, global variables, and linear memory. Supporting these additional features ensures that GenWasym can be applied to real-world Wasm programs. The implementation of these features still follows the semantics-based approach, and here we discuss the implementation of some of these features, including global variables, linear memory, and indirect control flow.

Global Variables

As described in Section 5, we have refactored the semantics by lifting the stack, environment, and path condition into mutable global states. To support WebAssembly global variables, we add a separate global component to the semantics. In GenWasym, WebAssembly globals are compiled into a C++ global data structure, and global-variable instructions (e.g., global.get and global.set) are translated into direct operations on it. As with the stack and environment, we use persistent data structures from Immer (Puente, 2017) to represent global state, enabling efficient snapshotting.

Linear Memory

Support for linear memory is essential for symbolic reasoning about realistic data structures, which are typically allocated in WebAssembly memory. In the official WebAssembly semantics, linear memory is modeled as a mapping from addresses to bytes. For concolic execution, we refine this model by representing each address as a pair of concrete and symbolic byte values.

WebAssembly provides memory operations over multiple data types, including 32-/64-bit integers and floating-point numbers. To handle them uniformly, we follow WASP and implement memory operations as byte-level operations on both concrete and symbolic memory. For example, i32.load reads four consecutive bytes and combines them into a 32-bit value, while i32.store decomposes a 32-bit value into four bytes and writes them back to consecutive addresses. In the implementation, GenWasym represents memory using persistent data structures, enabling efficient snapshotting.

Indirect Control Flow

WebAssembly indirect control flow instructions such as call_indirect allow the call target to be resolved at runtime rather than fixed statically. This mechanism helps compile higher-level languages with dynamic dispatch to WebAssembly. The WebAssembly standard assigns a unique index to each function, and a runtime global table stores these indices. The call_indirect instruction uses its operand to look up this table and resolve the target. Following the specification, GenWasym initializes a global table mapping WebAssembly function indices to C++ function pointers at program startup. This table is initialized when the compiled program starts and is used to resolve indirect calls at runtime. We compile each call_indirect instruction into a table lookup followed by a call to the resolved function.

Limitations

As a prototype implementation, GenWasym already supports a substantial subset of WebAssembly 2.0 (Rossberg, 2022), but it does not yet cover all features defined in the WebAssembly standard. GenWasym currently does not support several additional WebAssembly features, such as SIMD instructions, function references, and module import/export. Nevertheless, as long as the specification provides clear semantics for these features, extending GenWasym to support these features would be straightforward and requires moderate engineering effort.

8. Empirical Evaluation

This section evaluates the performance of GenWasym with respect to the following three questions:

  1. RQ1:

    How much speedup does compilation provide over interpretation-based approaches?

  2. RQ2:

    When snapshot and the heuristic are effective in GenWasym?

  3. RQ3:

    Is GenWasym effective in finding real bugs?

Environment and Setup

All experiments ran on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS with an AMD Ryzen 7 7735H CPU and 16 GB RAM. We used Z3 4.8.12 and compiled generated code with Clang 22.1.0 at -O3. For the baseline, we used WASP version 0.2.3, the latest release at submission time of this paper.

For performance measurement, we decompose the total wall-clock time into instruction-execution time and SMT-solving time. Our evaluation focuses on instruction execution, reporting the arithmetic mean over 5 runs for each benchmark. We also report end-to-end execution time (including time spent in SMT solvers) for completeness, although it depends on symbolic-expression encodings and query optimizations, which are beyond the scope of this paper. To validate the generated SMT queries and ensure the fairness of the comparison, we verify that the number of explored paths matches that of the baseline WASP (Marques et al., 2022).

Benchmarks

We evaluate against four groups of benchmarks, shown in Table 1. To assess performance on practical workloads, we adopt two benchmarks from prior work: (1) the B-Tree benchmark from WASP (Marques et al., 2022), and (2) the Collections-C test suites (srdja, n.d.), which exercise various data structures from the Gillian project (Santos et al., 2020). Compared with their original configurations in WASP, we use larger symbolic inputs and explore more paths for both the B-Tree benchmark (Marques et al., 2022) and the Collections-C benchmark (srdja, n.d.) to better approximate practical workloads. The B-Tree benchmark contains 26 cases, while the Collections-C benchmark contains 143 across 8 modules, yielding 169 cases in total.

We include two micro-benchmarks to understand the performance characteristics of snapshot reuse: (3) an arithmetic evaluator and (4) a quicksort implementation. These two benchmarks are designed to isolate the performance effects of snapshot reuse (RQ2). The quicksort benchmark is written in C and compiled to Wasm, whereas the arithmetic evaluator is written directly in Wasm. The arithmetic-evaluator benchmark contains 9 Wasm programs, each of which parses and evaluates a string-represented arithmetic expression. The programs vary in expression size, measured by the number of arithmetic operators, and the number of explored paths.

The quicksort benchmark varies both the input-array size and the number of symbolic elements. We initialize the symbolic inputs with either atomic symbolic variables or complex symbolic arithmetic expressions, allowing us to study how symbolic-state complexity affects snapshot reuse.

To answer RQ3, we use two Collections-C benchmarks from WASP (Marques et al., 2022) to evaluate bug-detection effectiveness. Each benchmark has two versions: a buggy version containing two known bugs and a correct version in which both bugs are fixed.

Baselines

There are several recent interpretation-based symbolic execution engines for WebAssembly, including Manticore (Mossberg et al., 2019), SeeWasm (He et al., 2024), WASP (Marques et al., 2022) and WASP’s successor Owi (Andrès et al., 2024). For RQ1, we choose to use WASP as the baseline for comparison, as it is the only tool among them implementing the same concolic execution semantics as GenWasym. Owi and Manticore both implement a general parallel symbolic execution semantics, which is not driven by concrete execution. SeeWasm constructs a control-flow graph for Wasm program, then symbolically explores the CFG using BFS or DFS strategy, without concrete inputs.

However, as these tools realize similar testing capabilities for end-users, their relative performance is worth noting to better understand where GenWasym would stand. On the same B-Tree benchmark, Owi with 1 worker reports similar performance comparable to WASP (0.8×0.8\times slowdown), while Owi with 24 workers achieves an average 4.1×4.1\times speedup over WASP (Andrès et al., 2024). In addition, WASP reports 5.4×5.4\times–26.2×26.2\times speedups over Manticore (Marques et al., 2022), whereas SeeWasm reports 1.2×1.2\times–4.8×4.8\times speedups over Manticore (He et al., 2024). Taken together, these published results from the literature suggest that WASP is a competitive baseline for our evaluation.

To the best of our knowledge, there currently exists no instrumentation-based concolic engine for Wasm, so we could not include such a baseline in our evaluation.

8.1. RQ1: GenWasym Performance Compared to Interpretation-Based Approaches

Method

To isolate the benefits of staging from snapshot-reuse, we disable snapshot-reuse in GenWasym for RQ1, forcing each execution to restart from the program entry, as in WASP. We report the mean instruction-execution time and end-to-end execution time, with a two-hour wall-clock timeout per run. For WASP, the measurements exclude WebAssembly module parsing.

We configure the B-Tree benchmark using two parameters: the numbers of ordered and unordered symbolic inputs, denoted by non_{o} and nun_{u}, respectively. The extended Collections-C benchmark contains nin_{i} test cases for each data structure, listed in Table 1. We compile all test cases to WebAssembly and perform concolic execution on the resulting modules. For every RQ1 benchmark, we ensure that GenWasym and WASP explore the same number of paths.

The two benchmark suites play complementary roles in assessing performance across synthetic and realistic workloads. The extended B-Tree benchmark provides a controlled setting for systematically varying the state-space by imposing different ordering constraints on symbolic inputs. For example, a>ba>b excludes inputs where a≤ba\leq b, reducing the feasible input space. Collections-C provides more realistic workloads: its Wasm programs are compiled from a C implementation of various collection data structures that are widely used in real-world applications.

Results

Table 1 shows the results. We compute the speedup of staging S𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑖𝑛𝑔S_{\mathit{staging}} as T𝑒𝑥𝑒𝑐WASP/T𝑒𝑥𝑒𝑐𝑛𝑜𝑟𝑒𝑢𝑠𝑒T_{\mathit{exec}}^{\mathit{\textsc{WASP}}}/T_{\mathit{exec}}^{\mathit{noreuse}}. We observe that GenWasym consistently and substantially outperforms WASP in instruction-execution time across all configurations of the extended B-Tree and Collections-C benchmarks (Table 1). On average, GenWasym achieves a 66.7×66.7\times speedup over WASP on the B-Tree benchmark, with the highest 652.5×652.5\times speedup excluding the timed-out configuration (no,nu)=(10,3)(n_{o},n_{u})=(10,3). On the Collections-C benchmark, GenWasym achieves a 3.9×3.9\times speedup. Overall, across 169 test programs spanning two benchmark groups, GenWasym achieves an average speedup of 33.4×33.4\times. On the arithmetic-evaluator benchmark and the quicksort benchmark, GenWasym achieves an average speedup of 21.6×21.6\times.

On the B-Tree benchmark, WASP exhibits increasingly severe slowdowns as execution time grows. We hypothesize that this degradation stems largely from its small-step interpretation and garbage collection (GC) in OCaml. The performance gains of GenWasym come primarily from three sources: (1) Compilation eliminates the interpretation overhead of repeatedly dispatching instructions. (2) By leveraging the Wasm CPS semantics (Wei et al., 2025), the generated C++ code translates control-flow instructions directly into function calls, whereas WASP evaluates control flow through administrative instructions. (3) And lastly, the generated code avoids GC and uses efficient data structures to represent execution state, including the stack and environment.

Summary

Figure 10(a) summarizes the speedup results for each benchmark group. Overall, the geometric mean of GenWasym’s speedups over WASP across all four benchmark groups is 29.4×29.4\times.

8.2. RQ2: When Are Snapshot Reuse and Our Heuristic Effective?

Method

To evaluate snapshot reuse and our heuristic, we compare configurations of GenWasym with these features enabled or disabled. In general, the net benefit of snapshot reuse depends on two factors: the execution it avoids and the cost of instantiating snapshots. Although the RQ1 benchmarks support a broad performance evaluation, they do not isolate this trade-off. We therefore use two controlled benchmarks (an arithmetic evaluator and quicksort) to vary these factors independently. For reference, we also report WASP’s performance.

The arithmetic-evaluator benchmark is parameterized by the input-expression AST size (n𝑛𝑜𝑑𝑒n_{\mathit{node}} in Table 1) and the number of explored paths. Increasing the expression size increases the execution depth of each path and thus the number of executed instructions. Because path forking occurs late in execution in this benchmark, increasing the number of paths would increase sharing in the execution tree, allowing snapshot reuse to skip more common execution.

Quicksort may reorder array elements but does not construct new concrete or symbolic values. We exploit this property to control symbolic-state complexity through the AST sizes of the symbolic inputs. Each symbolic input can be initialized as either an atomic symbolic variable or a complex symbolic arithmetic expression. Larger expressions make snapshots more expensive to copy and instantiate. Table 1 shows the benchmark parameters: the syntactic complexity of symbolic inputs n𝑐𝑜𝑚𝑝n_{\mathit{comp}}, the input array size n𝑠𝑖𝑧𝑒n_{\mathit{size}}, and the number of symbolic elements n𝑠𝑦𝑚n_{\mathit{sym}}. The remaining n𝑠𝑖𝑧𝑒−n𝑠𝑦𝑚n_{\mathit{size}}-n_{\mathit{sym}} elements are initialized with distinct concrete values. We define n𝑐𝑜𝑚𝑝n_{\mathit{comp}} as the sum of the syntactic sizes of all symbolic values in the array. For example, storing a 32-bit symbolic value xx as 4 bytes in the Wasm memory requires 4 SMT 𝖾𝗑𝗍𝗋𝖺𝖼𝗍h​i,l​o​(x)\mathsf{extract}_{hi,lo}(x) expressions which have size 2 each, so an atomic symbolic variable has size 8. We can deliberately construct symbolic states of arbitrary complexity by repeatedly applying arithmetic operations to the initial symbolic values.

Results

Table 1 shows the results. The columns T𝑒𝑥𝑒𝑐𝑛𝑜𝑟𝑒𝑢𝑠𝑒T_{\mathit{exec}}^{\mathit{noreuse}}, T𝑒𝑥𝑒𝑐𝑠𝑛𝑎𝑝𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑡T_{\mathit{exec}}^{\mathit{snapshot}}, and T𝑒𝑥𝑒𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑢𝑟𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑐T_{\mathit{exec}}^{\mathit{heuristic}} report instruction-execution times without snapshot reuse, with uniform snapshot reuse, and with heuristic snapshot reuse, respectively. We report three speedups to quantify the benefits of avoiding re-execution: S𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑖𝑛𝑔S_{\mathit{staging}}, the speedup of staging over the WASP baseline; S𝑠𝑛𝑎𝑝𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑡S_{\mathit{snapshot}}, the speedup of uniform snapshot reuse over no-reuse; and Sℎ𝑒𝑢𝑟𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑐S_{\mathit{heuristic}}, the speedup of heuristic snapshot reuse over no-reuse.

On the B-Tree and Collections-C benchmarks, both uniform and heuristic snapshot reuse yield modest average speedups of 1.1×1.1\times, compared to GenWasym with snapshot reuse disabled. Some configurations instead exhibit slight slowdowns, with S𝑠𝑛𝑎𝑝𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑡S_{\mathit{snapshot}} as low as 0.9×0.9\times on the Queue benchmark, and Sℎ𝑒𝑢𝑟𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑖𝑐S_{\mathit{heuristic}} as low as 0.9×0.9\times on the RingBuffer benchmark. Although snapshot reuse avoids re-executing shared prefixes, it does not always reduce the total execution time because the cost of creating and resuming snapshots is comparable to that of re-executing those prefixes.

On the arithmetic-evaluator benchmark, heuristic snapshot reuse achieves an average 4.8×4.8\times speedup over no-reuse. It also outperforms uniform snapshot reuse by an average of 1.7×1.7\times. Although snapshot incur overhead, its better reuse decisions consistently reduce overall execution time.

The quicksort results exhibit a different pattern. With atomic symbolic expressions as inputs (e.g., n𝑐𝑜𝑚𝑝≤102n_{\mathit{comp}}\leq 10^{2}), uniform snapshot reuse remains beneficial because snapshots can bypass shared execution prefixes at negligible resumption cost. With more complex symbolic states (e.g., n𝑐𝑜𝑚𝑝>104n_{\mathit{comp}}>10^{4}), however, uniform reuse slows execution relative to no-reuse, yielding an average S𝑠𝑛𝑎𝑝𝑠ℎ𝑜𝑡S_{\mathit{snapshot}} of 0.6×0.6\times. For short executions, the cost of copying and resuming snapshots containing large symbolic expressions outweighs the cost of re-executing the shared prefix. However, the heuristic effectively avoids these unfavorable cases, reusing snapshots only when the saved execution time justifies the overhead and yielding a 3.1×3.1\times speedup over no-reuse.

Summary

Uniform snapshot creation and restoration can outweigh the saved execution time, causing slowdowns in some cases. Our heuristic identifies these cases and makes more effective reuse decisions, consistently outperforming uniform snapshot reuse. Figure 10(b) shows the average speedups from snapshot reuse. Beyond staging’s 29.4×29.4\times speedup over WASP, uniform snapshot reuse adds 1.3×1.3\times speedup (i.e. 38.8×38.8\times vs WASP), and heuristics adds another 1.2×1.2\times speedup over uniform snapshot reuse (i.e., 44.9×44.9\times vs WASP).

8.3. RQ3: Is GenWasym effective in finding real bugs?

Method

To evaluate the effectiveness of GenWasym in detecting real bugs in practical programs, we conduct experiments on two buggy programs from Collections-C. These programs were previously used to evaluate the bug-finding effectiveness of WASP (Marques et al., 2022) and Gillian (Santos et al., 2020). Both contain memory-safety violations that may cause memory corruption and thus pose potential security risks. For our evaluation, we compile the Collections-C test cases from C to WebAssembly and run concolic execution on the resulting Wasm modules. We also run WASP as a reference baseline for comparison.

Results
